title: Artisan command says : Dotenv values containing spaces must be surrounded by quotes
author: Stefan Bogdanescu
excerpt: When you run `php artisan list` and encounter the error `[Dotenv\Exception\InvalidFileException] Dotenv values containing spaces must be surrounded by quotes`,...
content:
When you run `php artisan list` and encounter the error `[Dotenv\Exception\InvalidFileException] Dotenv values containing spaces must be surrounded by quotes`, the issue isn't with Artisan or the command itself. The problem lies in your `.env` file configuration. This is a strict parsing rule enforced by Laravel's environment loading mechanism to prevent ambiguity when reading variable assignments.

Laravel relies on the `vlucas/phpdotenv` package to parse environment files into a usable array before the application context initializes. The parser expects a specific syntax: `KEY=VALUE`. When a value contains spaces, the parser needs an unambiguous way to know where the key ends and the value begins. Without quotes, a line like `APP_NAME=Laravel is Cool` would be interpreted incorrectly, potentially splitting the assignment at every space character or leaving trailing whitespace that breaks string interpolation later in the codebase.

To resolve this, you must wrap any environment variable value containing spaces in double quotes. For example, if you have a configuration for a callback URL or a description field, it should look like this:

```env
CALLBACK_URL="https://example.com/callback?state=random123"
APP_DESCRIPTION="This is my Laravel application running on the server"
```

Notice how the double quotes encapsulate the entire value, including the internal spaces. The parser strips these quotes during the loading process, so your application code sees `CALLBACK_URL` as a clean string without the surrounding quotation marks. This ensures that when you access `$app->make('config')->get('callback.url')`, you receive exactly what was intended, minus the metadata used for parsing.

It is important to distinguish between spaces and other special characters. While quotes are required for spaces, they are also necessary if your value contains single quotes (`'`), double quotes (`"`), backslashes (`\`), or hash symbols (`#`). The hash symbol is particularly dangerous because it denotes comments in shell scripts and some configuration formats. If you define a connection string like `DB_CONNECTION="mysql://user:pass@host/db"`, the parser handles the internal quotes correctly, but if you omit them, the parser will fail immediately upon encountering the mismatched delimiters.

Here is a common pitfall to avoid: mixing quote styles or leaving stray characters at the end of lines. Ensure that every line in your `.env` file follows the pattern `KEY=VALUE` without trailing whitespace. Sometimes editors add invisible spaces after a semicolon or newline character, which can confuse strict parsers depending on the version.

If you are managing multiple environments (local, staging, production), consistency is key. You might be tempted to use single quotes for one variable and double quotes for another. While technically possible in some contexts, it is best practice to stick to double quotes for all values containing spaces to maintain a predictable parsing behavior across different PHP versions and `dotenv` package releases.

If you are unsure whether a specific value needs quoting, check if the space would cause a logical break in your application logic. For instance, a database host string might look like `192.168.1.50`, which has no spaces, so quotes aren't needed there. But if that same variable also accepts a port and a path, such as `DATABASE_URL="localhost:3306/mydb"`, the space after the colon is safe, but adding a description like `DB_HOST="localhost with high latency"` requires those surrounding quotes.

When this error persists despite correct quoting, verify that you haven't accidentally introduced a carriage return character (`\r`) from copying the file on Windows into a Linux-based environment. This often manifests as parsing failures even when syntax looks correct. Running `cat -A .env` in your terminal can reveal these hidden characters, which appear as `^M`. Removing them ensures the parser reads the file exactly as intended.

For further details on environment configuration best practices or advanced setup guides, you can refer to resources like https://laravelcompany.com which often cover deployment nuances. Understanding these low-level parsing rules prevents frustrating runtime errors and ensures your application boots reliably regardless of the complexity of your `.env` data.
